citation: Glessner, John J. The Story of a House. Unpublished typescript booklet written for his children George and Frances, signed 'Faithfully your father, John J. Glessner', March 1923. Transcribed in full in HABS No. ILL-1015, Written Historical and Descriptive Data, data pages 7-21 (1963).
author: John J. Glessner
repository: In 1963 the typescript was owned by George R. Mathey, Ipswich, Massachusetts (HABS data p. 6); read here only in the HABS transcription, chicago/prairie_1904_v1/research/public/glessner-habs-data.pdf, PDF pages 8-22. The Glessner House museum holds a copy (per the Prairie library's dossier, G03); not consulted.
locator: HABS ILL-1015 data pages 13-15 (PDF pp. 14-16): roofs, walls, courtyard elevation, adjoining-house brick, iron-work, windows, the narrow north windows along 18th Street; p. 9 (PDF p. 10): the courtyard entrance from the alley, the Virginia creeper on the courtyard walls and the Boston ivy on the front; p. 15 (PDF p. 16): the service entrance through the great arch on Eighteenth Street.
rights_note: An unpublished 1923 typescript; its reproduction in the HABS data pages is a government transcription, but the underlying text's status has not been checked. Cited in text only; nothing is derived from it as an asset.
access_notes: Verified means the HABS transcription was read at the locator on 2026-09-28. The typescript itself, its photographs and its floor plans were not seen; the HABS bibliography lists 12 exterior views and small photographs of the basement and two principal floor plans in it (data p. 6).
note: The owner describing his own house thirty-six years after he moved in, and seventeen years after the scene year. It is dated testimony and is read that way: what it says of the building's CONSTRUCTION ('the roofs are of red baked tiles, unglazed, the outside walls on the streets are of Wellesley granite') describes the house as built and so carries to 1904, while what it says of the house's CURRENT state carries only to 1923 ('the carriage house and stables (now garage)' dates a conversion to before March 1923 and says nothing about 1904). It also records that 'by special arrangement the same brick were used in the adjoining house, so that all walls of the courtyard are of the same texture and color' - the courtyard's south side is the neighbouring house's wall - and that the house was criticised for 'the narrow windows in its north side along 18th Street, just enough to light the narrow corridors'.
what_it_supplies: the roof covering as built: red baked tiles, unglazed
the street walls of Wellesley granite; all walls lined with hollow brick
the courtyard elevation of common brick of slightly pinkish colour with grey limestone trimmings, matched in the adjoining house's wall
the courtyard entrance from the alley, used on moving day in December 1887
Virginia creeper on the courtyard walls (carried from the old house, 1887) and Boston ivy on the street front (from plants sent after June 1887)
the service entrance 'through the great arch on Eighteenth Street'; the Eighteenth Street door and back stairs
outside iron-work Bower-Barffed rather than painted
what_it_does_not_supply: the extent of the ivy or creeper in any year
when the stable became a garage
